segments.text: If physical activity were a pill,
it would be the most prescribed medication in medicine.
Let's talk about why physical activity is so powerful,
because this isn't just about weight loss, aesthetics,
or chasing a certain body type.
Regular physical activity improves your cardiovascular
and muscular fitness, your bone health,
and lowers your risk of fracture.
It improves anxiety, depression,
and helps with overall mood regulation.
It improves your sleep quality and energy levels,
and it helps your self-esteem and cognitive functioning,
including reducing the risk of dementia.
It also plays a major role in preventing
and managing chronic disease.
Consistent movement lowers the risk of hypertension
and type 2 diabetes and is associated
with the lower incidence of multiple cancers,
including breast, colon, bladder, endometrial,
prostate, lung, stomach, and esophageal cancers.
Now let's zoom in on aerobic exercise specifically.
Aerobic activity lowers all cause mortality,
meaning all causes of death,
reduces the incidence of and death from cardiovascular disease, improves insulin sensitivity, lowers
your triglycerides, improves your sleep and overall quality of life.
This is why many major guidelines recommend 150 minutes per week of moderate intensity
exercise or 75 minutes of vigorous intensity exercise.
But here's where people get stuck.
They think it has to be intense, perfect, or all or nothing.
It doesn't.
Walking absolutely counts.
In fact, large population studies show that 7,000 steps to 12,000 steps per day is a sweet
spot where we see significant reductions in all-cause mortality, lower cardiovascular
risk, and improved metabolic health.
Beyond that range, the benefits tend to plateau, meaning more isn't always better, but if
you want to get more steps, have at it.
The goal is consistency, not extremes.
And steps matter in particular because they reflect total daily movement, not just a single
workout.
walking, errands going up and down your stairs pacing while you're on the phone
and everyday activity which is critical since as we mentioned prolonged
sedentary time independently increases your health risk. Movement isn't
punishment, it's protection. And in the next video we'll break down how to write
yourself a simple realistic cardio exercise prescription you can actually
stick to.
